document_meta.title: Rhode Island Wildlife Action Plan (RIWAP) 2025 Draft

orientation.summary: This is Rhode Island's 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan (RIWAP), a 10-year revision of the state's wildlife conservation strategy produced by RIDEM. The document engages substantially with climate change as a cross-cutting threat, noting documented warming trends, sea level rise, and projected future conditions for Rhode Island, and explicitly treats climate change as compounding other threats. Range shifts are mentioned explicitly in a few passages: one notes that climate pressures are causing species range shifts while development may inhibit such movement, another discusses SLAMM-modeled salt marsh migration, and one passage about Conservation Opportunity Areas invokes corridors that allow species to shift in response to climate change. The document performs its own synthesis and mapping (COA mapping, habitat condition assessments) but largely relies on referenced analyses from partners such as TNC, URI, and NECASC for climate-specific modeling and vulnerability work.

evidence_index.text: Average annual temperature has increased by about 4° F between 1895 and 2023, faster than global mean temperature and that of the Northeast generally (+2.5° F). The ocean region next to RI is experiencing rapid warming as well; the Gulf of Maine is among the fastest warming ocean regions globally.

evidence_index.text: Application of SLAMM (Sea Level Affecting Marshes Model) modeling at several federal wildlife refuges in the Northeast projected that the initial impact of sea level rise will be an increase in salt marsh (saline) habitats at the expense of brackish habitats (Grund and Walberg 2013).

evidence_index.text: In 2015, SLAMM modeling was published for the entire Rhode Island coast with similar impacts indicated and the degree of brackish marsh loss dependent on the accessibility of adjacent upland and/or freshwater wetland sites for inland marsh migration.

evidence_index.text: Because of their rarity and limited extent, brackish marsh communities are extremely vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, especially rising sea level.

evidence_index.text: Climate models identify 2035-2040 as the critical point when future scenario projections begin to diverge dramatically depending on emissions. In a medium emissions scenario, by 2100 RI is projected to experience as much as an additional up to 7˚F warming a tenfold increase in days with temperatures above 95˚F

evidence_index.text: changes in marine species phenology are being observed in Rhode Island marine waters; for example, residency time of warm-water species is increasing. Additionally, increasing CO 2 concentrations have driven changes in pH, leading to ocean acidification. This restricts growth and reduces survivorship of shellfish, crustaceans, and other species with carbonate-based body structures.

niche_models.absence_note: SLAMM is a habitat change model for marshes under sea level rise scenarios, which is more closely related to niche/habitat suitability modeling than other categories. It was applied to RI coastal areas. Habitat suitability models are also referenced as a future development goal for marine species. However, the main application of SLAMM described here is for habitat-level modeling, not species distribution modeling per se. Score of 1 as SLAMM results are referenced for habitat projections (applied to RI's coast) and species distribution/habitat suitability models are referenced as a planned future tool.

time_bound_and_monitoring.absence_note: The document describes a 10-year revision cycle, annual reporting through TRACS, and a 5-year review cycle, which represents time-bound plan-level structure. However, the codebook requires time-binding at the action level (specific deadlines on individual actions) to score higher than 1. The action urgency categories ('Initiate immediately,' 'Initiate within 5 years,' etc.) are noted in the action descriptor table, which gives urgency framing to actions, but effectiveness monitoring tied to specific range-shift actions is not operationalized at that level in the text reviewed. Score 1 for plan-level deadlines and adaptive management principles.
